title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation Extension
summary: Describes a TLS extension for application-layer protocol negotiation during the handshake. When several application protocols share the same port, it lets the client and server agree which one to use.

plainLanguage.summary: ALPN lets a TLS client and server agree on an application protocol during the handshake. The choice uses the existing handshake rather than adding network round-trips.

questions: how does alpn work in tls
how does tls choose between http/1.1 and http/2
subtitle: Negotiates the application protocol during the TLS handshake without adding network round-trips.

tldr.problem: A server can support several application protocols on the same port. The client and server need to agree which protocol to use for a connection.
tldr.mechanism: The client lists supported protocols in an extension to ClientHello. The server selects one and returns it in an extension to ServerHello.
tldr.outcome: ALPN places protocol selection in the TLS handshake. RFC 7301 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8447.

today: RFC 7301 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2014. It has been updated by RFC 8447.

sections.title: Why Negotiate a Protocol in TLS
sections.content:
Application protocols can share a server-side port, so a client and server need to select one for each connection. RFC 7301 defines Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) as a TLS extension for that choice.

The client and server exchange the choice within the TLS handshake, avoiding extra network round-trips. The RFC says a server can also use the negotiated protocol when selecting a certificate.
sections.plainLanguage: When one port supports several application protocols, the two sides need to choose one. ALPN carries that choice in the TLS handshake.

sections.title: The ALPN Extension Data
sections.content:
The client can include extension type application_layer_protocol_negotiation(16) in ClientHello. Its ProtocolNameList contains non-empty protocol identifiers as byte strings, ordered from most to least preferred. Each name is 1 to 255 bytes, and the list is 2 to 65535 bytes.

The server's response uses the same structure, but its list must contain exactly one protocol name. The RFC requires that protocol names not be truncated.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends a preference-ordered list of protocol identifiers. The server returns one identifier that it selected.

sections.title: Where ALPN Appears in the Handshake
sections.content:
The client places the ALPN extension in ClientHello, and a server that supports a suitable choice can return the extension in ServerHello. The RFC describes this for both full and abbreviated handshakes; ALPN does not add new handshake messages.

ALPN establishes a property of the connection, not the session. When a connection resumes, the previous ALPN values are irrelevant; the parties use the values in the new handshake.
sections.plainLanguage: ALPN information travels in the ClientHello and ServerHello messages. A resumed connection negotiates the protocol again in its new handshake.

sections.title: How the Server Selects a Protocol
sections.content:
The server is expected to keep its own preference-ordered list. It should select its most preferred protocol that also appears in the client's list.

If the server supports none of the protocols that the client offered, it sends the fatal no_application_protocol alert, whose description value is 120. Once selected, the protocol is definitive for the connection until renegotiation; the server must not use a different protocol for application data.
sections.plainLanguage: The server chooses a protocol that both sides support. If there is no shared choice, the server sends an error alert and ends the handshake.

sections.title: Visible Protocol Names and Security
sections.content:
The server's selected ALPN protocol is sent in plaintext. The RFC says ALPN does not change the security of TLS session establishment or application data, but the selected protocol is visible to observers.

In TLS 1.2 and earlier, the client also sends its offered identifiers in the clear. The RFC warns that identifiers could reveal personal information or enable profiling, and says such identifiers should not be used where they are visible in plaintext.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocol identifiers can be visible to observers during the handshake. Identifiers that reveal personal or sensitive information should not be sent in the clear.

sections.title: Protocol Identifier Registry
sections.content:
The RFC assigns extension type 16 to ALPN and creates the ALPN Protocol IDs registry. Each registration includes the protocol name, the exact sequence of identifying bytes, and a reference to its specification.

The registry uses Expert Review. Initial entries include http/1.1 and spdy/1, spdy/2, and spdy/3.
sections.plainLanguage: An official registry records each protocol name and the bytes that identify it. Expert review is required for new entries.
